Guide

Spoon, fingers, or both

Purées, finger foods, and a mixture of the two can all feed a baby well. The arguments about identity are louder than the evidence.

Findings

The method is less important than iron, texture, and responsive feeding. A baby can be spoon-fed, can self-feed soft pieces, or can do both in the same week.
Finger foods did not raise choking in a trial that taught safe shapes. Gagging was common. Choking was not increased when families were shown which shapes to avoid.
Smooth food has an expiry date. By eight or nine months a baby should be moving to mash and soft pieces. Staying on thin purée is the avoidable risk.

Three workable approaches

Spoon feeding lets you offer iron-rich meats and lentils in a smooth form while chewing is still new. Finger foods let a baby practise grip and control the pace. Most families end up mixing them, and that is a legitimate method rather than a compromise.

Baby-led weaning, as a slogan, sometimes leaves out iron or keeps meals so plain that a baby fills up on fruit. The studies that found baby-led feeding safe were studies in which families were told to include iron foods and to avoid round, hard, and coin-shaped pieces.

What the BLISS trial showed

The Baby-Led Introduction to Solids trial in New Zealand compared a supported baby-led approach with usual spoon feeding. There was no evidence of more choking. Gagging, which is noisy and protective, was part of normal learning.

That result does not mean every hard marketed biscuit is safe. It means soft strips, flakes of fish, and well-cooked vegetables, offered sitting upright, were comparable in risk to spoon feeding.

Move the texture on

At the start, food can be smooth or naturally soft. By about eight months, mash with soft lumps and foods the fist can hold. By about a year, the child should be eating family textures, with the salt still kept off their portion.

A blender is optional. A fork is enough for banana, avocado, and baked flesh. Blenders whip in air; if a baby is windy afterwards, stir the purée and let it stand before serving.
